# <img src="man/figures/variplex-wordmark.svg" alt="variplex" height="48"/> <img src="man/figures/logo.svg" align="right" height="139" alt="variplex logo"/>

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/rheradio/variplex/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/rheradio/variplex/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

A variability model lists the features that a configurable system offers and the constraints among them. Constraints
combine: if a feature requires a second one, and the second excludes a third, then the first also excludes the third,
although nobody wrote so. In large models, most relationships between features are written nowhere, yet engineers who
plan changes, review models, validate configurations or test releases depend on them.

variplex makes these relationships explicit, in two steps:

1. **It builds the graphs.** variplex compiles a model, once, into graphs of its *strong relationships*: every
   relationship between two features that holds in all the valid configurations, written in the model or not.
2. **It analyses the graphs.** More than a hundred functions answer the questions that engineers ask about a model,
   from one feature to the whole model and its versions, without calling a solver again. Every function returns a
   tibble.

## What the graphs are

For two features A and B of a model, variplex finds three kinds of strong relationships, each a graph:

| Graph | Link | Meaning |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **requires** | A → B | every valid configuration with A also has B |
| **excludes** | A — B | no valid configuration has both A and B |
| **at least one** | A ⋯ B | no valid configuration lacks both |

The nodes are the *variable* features, those in some valid configurations and not in others. *Core* features, in every
configuration, and *dead* ones, in none, are reported apart; abstract features, which only name groups of the tree,
are left out.

Take the Mi Band 3, a fitness band that comes with the package. Its
[feature model](https://github.com/rheradio/variplex/blob/main/inst/extdata/miband3_realized.uvl) is a tree with five cross-tree
constraints; it has 8 core features and 11 variable ones. Its graphs have 21 dependencies, 10 conflicts and 3
at-least-one links, and only 11 of these 34 links are written in the model as a tree edge, a group or a constraint
between two features. The others arise as constraints combine. For instance, every band with Bluetooth 4.2 has a
heart-rate sensor, yet no constraint says so: it follows from a constraint over three features, the Bluetooth group
and a constraint on a fourth one.

<img src="man/figures/README-miband3-model.svg" alt="The feature model of the Mi Band 3" width="100%"/>

*The feature model of the Mi Band 3: a tree of mandatory, optional and alternative features, and five cross-tree
constraints (c1 to c5). Core features are shaded; five of them are grouped in one box.*

```{r graphs-figure, include = FALSE}
library(variplex)
band <- vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"), or_graph = TRUE)
vp_plot(band, file = "man/figures/README-graphs.svg")
vp_plot(vp_minimal(band), file = "man/figures/README-minimal.svg")
```

<img src="man/figures/README-graphs.svg" alt="The three graphs of the Mi Band 3" width="100%"/>

*The graphs of the Mi Band 3: requires (blue arrows), excludes (red dashes) and at least one (green dots). Screen,
OLED and CapacityButton, always selected together, are one node.*

Because each link joins just two features, the graphs are **plain graphs**, which pays off twice:

- **Engineers can read them.** Each link is one simple fact that can be drawn and checked against the requirements.
  The readings are immediate: Screen, OLED and CapacityButton are the most required features; BT40 is the most
  incompatible, excluding 7 features; MovementFilter forces 4 features and forbids 3.
- **Graph algorithms apply to them.** Centrality finds the features on which most others depend, communities the
  parts of a model that separate teams could configure, and paths explain why two features cannot go together. Unlike
  a drawing, these analyses scale to models with thousands of features, such as the Kconfig models of Linux.
  `vp_igraph()` hands the graphs to igraph for any other algorithm.

The graphs are synthesized once using a SAT solver and an auxiliary graph called Modal Implication Graph (MIG), which
takes seconds to minutes even on the largest models. The model can be a feature model in
[UVL](https://universal-variability-language.github.io/), or the Boolean formula (DIMACS) of a model written in any
other notation, such as the Kconfig files of the Linux kernel translated by KMax, KConfigReader or KconfigSampler.

## What the graphs answer

Once the graphs are built, most questions become lookups or classic graph algorithms. Four everyday engineering tasks
show the idea:

| Task | Question | Functions |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Impact analysis | What does selecting or removing a feature force and forbid? | `vp_consequences()`, `vp_requirements()`, `vp_conflicts_of()` |
| Model review | From which few relationships do all the others follow? Why does a dependency or conflict hold? | `vp_minimal()`, `vp_explain_requires()`, `vp_explain_conflict()` |
| Configuration validation | Can these decisions go together? If not, why? | `vp_partial_configuration()`, `vp_can_go_together()` |
| Release and test management | What did a release change in meaning, not just in text? Which pairs of features must be retested? | `vp_compare()`, `vp_changed_links()`, `vp_edit_type()` |

Beyond them, the functions cover the measures of each feature, the layers and hierarchy of a model, the whole model,
conflicts, configuration and teams, combinatorial testing, network patterns, and the evolution of a model through its
versions. `vp_functions()` lists them by topic.

## Installation

```r
install.packages("variplex")
```

Nothing has to be installed outside R. To draw the graphs, install also the suggested packages DiagrammeR (and
DiagrammeRsvg and rsvg to save drawings as SVG, PDF or PNG). The development version is on GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("rheradio/variplex")
```

## Example

Build the graphs of the Mi Band 3:

```{r example}
library(variplex)

band <- vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"), or_graph = TRUE)
band
```

**Impact analysis.** A cheaper band without a screen is planned. What does it touch? Besides the features under the
screen in the tree, it loses both versions of Bluetooth Low Energy, and must use classic Bluetooth:

```{r impact}
vp_consequences(band, deselected = "Screen")
```

**Model review.** The minimal form keeps the few links from which all the others follow, each through a path, so that
a review can start from them; the explanations trace any link back to them:

```{r review}
vp_minimal(band)
vp_explain_conflict(band, "MovementFilter", "BT40")
```

<img src="man/figures/README-minimal.svg" alt="The minimal form of the graphs of the Mi Band 3" width="100%"/>

**Configuration validation.** A customer orders a band with a movement filter and Bluetooth 4.2. It cannot be built,
and the graphs say why:

```{r validation}
vp_can_go_together(band, list(c("MovementFilter", "BLEv42")))$reasons
```

**Release and test management.** The model planned before the release had fewer constraints than the released one.
The release only gained links, so it restricted the model; each gained link rules out a pair of decisions, so those
pairs no longer need testing:

```{r release}
planned <- vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_planned.uvl"), or_graph = TRUE)
vp_compare(planned, band)
```

```r
vp_plot(band)                                      # draw the graphs, with DiagrammeR
```

## How far the graphs can be trusted

The graphs know everything that can be said about pairs of features, and nothing more:

- Every answer about one or two features (is it core? does A require B? can A and B go together?) is **exact**.
- When a question involves more features, such as whether a partial configuration can be completed, a **"no" is always
  right**, and it comes with its cause.
- A **"yes" can be wrong**, though rarely: a rule that ties three or more features at once without forcing anything on
  any two of them is in no graph. If a battery cannot power NFC, the heart-rate sensor and the touch screen at once,
  the graphs stay the same, and they accept the three together.

`vignette("limits-theory")` proves these guarantees and measures how often a "yes" is wrong on real models.

## Built on

variplex is built upon two tools developed by Rubén Heradio and colleagues:

- [Strong4VM](https://github.com/rheradio/strong4vm), which extracts the graphs of strong relationships from a
  variability model ([Heradio et al., 2026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.softx.2026.102663));
- BoneDigger, a backbone solver, which finds the literals that hold in every valid configuration of a model.

Their C++ code, with the SAT solver Glucose, is compiled into the package, so nothing has to be installed outside R.

Start with `vignette("variplex")`. The other vignettes go through the results (`vignette("graphs")`) and every
